column2: kvas

My great body has troubled me since I was a child, and now it has grown past what my legs can carry. I can barely cross a room without a servant at my elbow, and some mornings it takes all my strength just to lift my head from the pillow.
No! I will train every day until it obeys me!
Why does [Root.Religion.GetRandomEvilGodName] mock me so?

Since I was small my body has grown and grown, and I have hardened it with every inch. Now I stand like a tower among my people, broad as a door and with the muscles of a [Root.GetRegionalFerociousAnimal]. Men step aside when I walk into a hall.
How is the weather down there?

I am no longer young, and still my body will not stop growing. My skin thickens, my voice deepens, my joints ache and a headache sits behind my eyes that never quite leaves. I have never looked more fearsome, and I have never felt weaker. Something in me is wearing thin.
How long can a body like this last?

[concerned_relative.GetFirstName] tore the cup from my hand as I reached for more [Root.GetCharDrink] and dashed it against the wall. "You are killing yourself!" [concerned_relative.GetSheHe] shouted, eyes wet. "Stop, if not for yourself then for your blood."
I will try. For you.
You try to give up the drink. It may make you ill.
How dare you tell me what to do?
You make no attempt to stop drinking.
[concerned_relative.GetFirstName] has died, and there is no one now to take the cup from my hand. Perhaps that is reason enough to put it down myself, in [concerned_relative.GetHerHis] memory.
Not another drop, for [concerned_relative.GetHerHim].
I need the drink to bear it.

I have barely touched the [Root.GetCharDrink] in weeks, and [concerned_relative.GetFirstName] noticed. "You look so much better," [concerned_relative.GetSheHe] said, taking my hands. "Your colour is back. I knew you could do it."
I did it for you.

I woke today wanting a drink more than I have ever wanted anything. I shake, I sweat, and my stomach will not keep down even bread. But I will not give in. [concerned_relative.GetFirstName] would never forgive me.
This is supposed to be good for me?
I tried, I truly did. Then I found a jug of [Root.GetCharDrink] left out one night and drank it to the bottom. No one would have known, if a servant had not told [concerned_relative.GetFirstName].
I just cannot do it.
Every doorway in this place was built for smaller folk, and I strike my head on nearly all of them. The servants hide their smiles badly, and the children have made a game of counting the bumps.
I will wait until no one is watching.
It hurts, but it builds character.

I know a shadow has been on you of late, my court physician [physician.GetFirstName] said, and held out a little clay cup. "Drink this. It may lift the darkness, though I will not lie to you: it does not agree with everyone." The grey draught smells faintly of ash and bitter roots.
Anything to feel better.
You drink the draught, whatever it does to you.
I am not drinking that.
It was hard to see at first, but now there is no doubt: my [GetFromRelation] [From.GetFirstName] favours the left hand. It might be wise to correct the habit before it sets.

It was hard to see at first, but now there is no doubt: my [GetFromRelation] [From.GetFirstName] favours the left hand, the sinister hand. The priests say it is the hand the Dark Gods reach for first, and that a child who leads with it leads with an open door. This must not take root.

It was not hard to see that my [GetFromRelation] [From.GetFirstName] favours the left hand, as I do. I know what it costs, the whispers, the clumsy swordplay against right-handed masters. Should I spare the child that, and correct it while I still can?
The left hand is the hand of the Dark Gods!
Teach §Y[From.GetFirstName]§! what the holy texts say of the sinister hand.
The right hand is simply more practical.
Teach §Y[From.GetFirstName]§! how a left-handed fighter is hampered in the shield wall.
The child is fine as [From.GetSheHe] is.

My [GetFromRelation] [From.GetFirstName] is angry with me. [From.GetSheHeCap] says I must always use my right hand, for everything, or [From.Religion.GetHighGodName] will turn from me and something darker will take my left.

My [GetFromRelation] [From.GetFirstName] told me to use my right hand instead of my left, always. [From.GetSheHeCap] says it will serve me well when I am older and have to hold a sword and shield like everyone else.
Of course, [GetFromRelation]! (Lie)
Very well, [GetFromRelation]. I will do as you say.
No! I like my left hand!

[From.GetFirstName], that sly little wretch, had me believing [From.GetSheHe] had given up [From.GetHerHis] left hand. This morning I overheard [From.GetHerHim] boasting of the trick to [From.GetHerHis] playmates!
How dare [From.GetSheHe]!
A dutiful [From.GetBoyGirl], [From.GetFirstName] has done as I asked and trained [From.GetHerselfHimself] to the right hand.
Good.
The gall of [From.GetFirstName]! [From.GetSheHeCap] refused me to my face, and goes on using [From.GetHerHis] left hand for everything [From.GetSheHe] does.
Outrageous!

The sky lit up white and the ground shook as a falling star crashed down into my [Root.GetVoiceGarden]. My people dug it out of the smoking pit: a lump of dark, cold metal unlike any our smiths have seen, heavy as lead and bright as silver where the spade scraped it.

A streak of fire split the night sky in two, and for a moment the whole court swore it saw twin tails, like the comet that heralded Sigmar. Then the ground shook as the star crashed down into my [Root.GetVoiceGarden]. My people dug out a lump of dark, cold metal, bright as silver where the spade scraped it. The priests are already calling it a sign.

A star fell last night and struck the mountainside above my hold. The miners dug it out by morning and laid it before me: star-iron, cold and black and heavier than gromril. The oldest runesmith ran his thumb along it and went quiet. Such metal is not seen once in a dozen lifetimes.

The sky-rock fell, fell! Green fire, a great boom, and it crashed into the burrows right above my warren. The clanrats who dug it out are already sick and twitching, and that can mean only one thing. Warpstone, a great fat lump of it, and it is mine-mine! Unless someone else squeaks first.

A big shiny rock fell out da sky and nearly squashed da camp. Took ten boyz to drag it out da hole, an' two of 'em got burned. Da Mek reckons it's proper good metal. Da Shaman reckons Gork frew it at us. Or Mork. Maybe both.

The sky split and a burning stone fell among my tents, as if the gods had flung it. When the smoke cleared the rock glowed a sick green at its heart and the dogs would not go near it. Warpstone, the stuff of the Realm of Chaos itself. My shamans say it is a gift, and that gifts are tests.

A falling star crashed into the grounds of my keep last night, and my servants dragged it in before dawn. A lump of cold, dark metal, bright as silver where the spade scraped it. The living would call it an omen. I call it a fine thing to make a blade from, and I have time enough to wait for the smiths.
This metal will make a legendary blade!
You set your smiths to forge a weapon from the star-metal.
A gift of [Root.Religion.GetHighGodName]. It goes to the temple.
It is only metal. Sell it, and quickly.
Hoard the warpstone. Its power is mine.

Weeks after the star fell into my [Root.GetVoiceGarden], the smiths have finished the weapon I ordered from its metal. I turn it in the light and it seems to hold a faint glow of its own. It came down from the heavens, and now it is in my hand.

The runesmiths have finished. The blade forged from the star-iron is plain to look at, as all true Dawi work is, but it rings when it is struck like a bell in the deep halls. The longbeards who saw it come out of the forge say it will outlast my grandchildren's grandchildren.
Da Mek finally finished bashin' da sky-rock into a choppa. It's big, it's shiny, it's sharp on da killin' end, an' it glows a bit in da dark. Best choppa in da whole WAAAGH!, an' it's mine.
The blade forged from the star-metal is finished. The smiths who made it are not well, and the edge has a faint green sheen that never quite leaves it. It is sharp, and it hungers, and it is mine.
A glorious weapon.
If I want to find a good husband, I must look my best, and so I have taken pains over it: oils, combs, the right gowns, rest. It has not been easy, but I think I am looking better every day.

If I want to find a good wife, I must look my best, and so I have taken pains over it: the barber, the tailor, a bath more often than the priests think healthy. It has not been easy, but I think I am looking better every day.
I want to look my best for my beloved spouse, and so I have taken pains over it. It has not been easy, but with care I think I look better every day.
If I want my sweet words to work, I must look my very best. Nobody falls for a toad, however well it talks. It has not been easy, but with care I think I look better every day.
Was there ever any doubt?
All these days out in the wilds are good for my health, but not for my looks. Every night I come home with mud to the knees, burrs in my hair and the smell of wet hounds on everything I own.
My training has made me strong and quick with a blade, but it has not been kind to my face. My skin is rough and weathered, and blotched with old bruises and small scars I no longer remember earning.
I cannot be seen like this!
So what? Looks do not matter.

A cold draught wakes me in the dead of night. My window stands open, and beside my bed is a hooded figure, still as a statue. "It is written in your stars," it says, in a voice like wind in the grass. "Go up into the mountains, alone, and watch the sky. The heavens have a gift for you."

A cold draught wakes me in the dead of night. My window stands open, and a spellsinger I do not know sits on the sill, her face hidden under a hood of leaves. "The trees have dreamed of you," she whispers. "Climb above the forest, alone, and watch the sky. Something falls for you alone to find."

A cold draught wakes me in the dead of night. My window stands open, and a woman in a pale hooded gown stands at the foot of my bed. A damsel of the Lady, though no damsel I have ever met. "The Lady has seen you in the waters," she says. "Go up into the mountains, alone, and watch the sky."
Speak. I am listening.
The prophecy sends you up into the mountains to watch for a sign.
Guards! Seize this mad intruder!

Frozen, footsore and half certain I have lost my wits, I reach a high peak at last. I am cursing myself for trusting a stranger in the night when a bright light streaks across the sky and falls into the forest at the mountain's roots.
I must follow the sign.
Follow the light alone, wherever it leads.
Those woods are deep and dangerous.
Go home and gather a search party first.
The stranger's words follow me into my dreams. However I try, I cannot let go of that prophecy, whispered by a madman in my own bedchamber.
My peace of mind depends on it. I will go.
Go up into the mountains as the prophecy said.
My mind has been poisoned. This is a trap!
You trust nothing for a while, not even your own instincts.
A Prophecy Foretold

After a day and half a night pushing through the thick forest, I come to a moonlit glade with a small pool shining silver at its end. Beside the pool lies a unicorn. It is barely breathing, and a black-fletched arrow, crude beastman work, stands in its flank. Silver blood seeps into the moss. As I kneel, it looks at me once and is still.\n\nI cannot bring the creature home whole, and I cannot leave such a wonder for the crows.
It deserves a proper burial.
Cup my hands and drink the silver blood.
Save its shining mane.
Cut the horn and bring it home.
We reached the forest a week later and searched it for days. We found nothing, no crater, no ash, no sign of the light that fell. Still, a light in the sky must mean something.
A sign of blessing on my rule.
I can no longer tell whether the glade was real or a dream. But ever since I buried the unicorn, I catch a faint silver glimmer of myself in other people's eyes.
And they seem to hold me higher for it.
Unicorn Horn
The spiral horn of a unicorn that died in a moonlit glade. It is cool to the touch on the hottest day, and wounds bound near it are said to close clean.
[renaming_target.Culture.GetName] Inquisition
[renaming_target.Culture.GetName] Raiders
Troubled Sleep

I really must ask my [bear_character.GetRootRelation] [bear_character.GetFirstName] to take rooms somewhere other than right beside my own. I love [bear_character.GetHerHim] dearly, but [bear_character.GetHerHis] snoring shakes the shutters, and I have not slept a full night in weeks.
I will ask [bear_character.GetFirstName] to move.
It would be rude to insist.
A Hairy Situation

I brushed past [bear_character.GetFirstName] on the way to the stables this afternoon. It was an impolite thought, but the closeness left me struck by just how very hairy my [bear_character.GetRootRelation] is. On the backs of the hands. On the neck. Everywhere, really.
Good thing it does not run in the family.
Well, it must be practical in winter.
Tongue-Tied

[bear_character.GetFirstName] is known as a [bear_character.GetManWoman] of few words. No words, in fact, unless one counts the grunting. They say silence is golden, but sometimes a [Root.GetManWoman] needs a proper conversation!
I will seek [Root.Spouse.GetFirstName]'s company instead.
I will seek [family_member.GetFirstName]'s company instead.
I will seek the priests' counsel instead.
The Honey Thief

A mysterious honey thief has been plaguing the court. Every few nights every pot of honey in the kitchens vanishes, the larder doors hang open and the jars lie smashed and licked clean. So far no one has caught the culprit, though the cooks swear they heard a contented snuffling.
My Marshal will find the thief.
My Spymaster will get to the bottom of this.
Sin is its own punishment.
A Poignant Portrait

[bear_character.GetFirstName] sat for a portrait this week. The colours are vivid, but poor [bear_character.GetFirstName]'s nose came out long and black and oddly damp-looking. I meant to complain to the painter about his sense of proportion, but come to think of it, [bear_character.GetFirstName] does have a remarkably generous nose.
We all have our flaws.
Some might call it stately.
Bearly Legal

At the latest banquet, after four pots of stew, three whole trout and a shank of lamb, [bear_character.GetFirstName] was lumbering off to bed as usual when [bear_character.GetHerHis] robes caught on the rough edge of a table. Before anyone could help, the cloth tore straight up to the collar, leaving poor [bear_character.GetFirstName] bare before the whole hall.\n\nIf that were not scandal enough, the guests fell silent at an astonishing truth: [bear_character.GetFirstName] was very clearly not a [bear_character.GetManWoman] at all. [bear_character.GetFirstName] was a bear.
Ursun walks among us! My house is blessed!
This is the work of some foul sorcerer!
This is unbearable!
Waking up, everything is back to normal. Perhaps it was all a dream...
Has [bear_character.GetSheHe] always been a bear?
That explains all the missing honey...
It will eat me! Unless I eat it first...
Shoot it and mount its head on the wall.
Send for a Court Sage
A wise ruler keeps a wiser counsellor. Send word across your lands for a holy sage of your faith to come and guide you.
Court Sage
The ruler's spiritual counsellor, a holy sage of the faith.
The search for a sage begins
Messengers ride out to the temples, the hermitages and the holy roads with word that I seek a sage to counsel me. It may take some time to find one worthy of the court.
Let them search far and wide.

My messengers have returned with [court_sage.GetTitledFirstName], a priest of Verena, goddess of learning and justice. He carries an owl-headed staff and a satchel of books, and he says that Verena's wisdom is wasted on those who will not listen. I intend to listen.

My messengers found [court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] at a lonely shrine of the Lady beside a mountain spring. The hermit has kept the shrine for twenty years and speaks little, but when he does speak, every knight in the hall falls silent.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has come to court barefoot and in rags, a holy wanderer who has walked the oblast from the Lynsk to the Tobol. The boyars sneer at the starets' filthy feet, but the common folk kneel as he passes, and he looks at me as though he can see straight through to my soul.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName], a scholar of the Prophets who has studied in the great libraries of Martek and Kufra, has accepted my invitation. He has memorised every word of the Prophets and has never once been known to flatter a sultan.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has journeyed from the far east, a sage of the Celestial Court who once advised the ministers of the Dragon Emperor himself. He bows low, sips his tea and tells me that a ruler who cannot govern himself cannot govern anything at all.
Welcome to my court, wise one.
[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] finds me with a cup in my hand again and gently takes it away. A ruler who drowns his wits in wine, the sage says, cannot complain when his enemies outthink him.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] watches the dancers, the musicians and the endless banquets with a weary face. A life spent chasing pleasure, the sage tells me, is a life spent running from something. What am I running from?

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has noticed how many visitors come to my bedchamber at night. The sage warns me that a ruler ruled by desire is the easiest of all to manipulate, and that my enemies have surely noticed too.

At the evening meal [court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] eats a little bread and watches me empty a third plate. Afterwards the sage tells me that a body is a gift of the gods, and that I treat mine like a pig trough.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has seen me count my gold twice in one day. The sage reminds me that no ruler has ever taken a single coin into the grave, and that the faithful remember a generous hand far longer than a full treasury.
[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] hears me complain once again about the wealth of a rival. Envy, the sage says, is a poison we drink in the hope that someone else will die of it.
My temper broke again today, and the servants fled from my shouting. [court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] waits until I am calm, then tells me that anger is a fire that burns the one who carries it first.
[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has been watching me accept the praise of my courtiers. The sage observes that every great house that ever fell was proud the day before.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has heard of my latest judgement and shakes his head. A ruler's word must be a rock, the sage says, not a weathervane. My people cannot obey laws that change with my moods.
[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has heard me mock the priests again. The sage does not argue. He only asks what I would put in the place of faith, if every temple in my realm emptied tomorrow.
[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] has seen what is done in my dungeons at my order. The sage tells me quietly that the gods weigh every cruelty, and that my scales are growing very heavy.

I have doubled my guards again and had my food tasted three times. [court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] tells me that a ruler who trusts no one soon finds that no one trusts him, and then his fears come true.
[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] rode past the stakes outside my gates this morning and has not eaten since. The sage asks me plainly what kind of god I think would bless a lord who rules by terror.
You are right. I will try to do better.
Your advice is noted. Now leave me.
How dare you lecture me? Guards!
Strange stories reach me about [court_sage.GetTitledFirstName]. The servants say the sage was seen in a tavern last night, roaring drunk and singing songs no holy man should know.
I will look into this myself.
Servants' gossip. I trust my sage.

I went down to the tavern in disguise and found [court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] at the card table, dice in one hand, a harlot on the knee and a pile of my own silver on the table. Whatever the sage is, a holy one is not it.
Enough. Bring the fraud before me.
Deal me in.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] stands before my court, sober at last and pale as milk. The sage has no holy learning at all, only a quick tongue and a good memory for the scriptures. I have been played for a fool, and everyone knows it.
To the dungeon with you.
Get out of my lands and never return.
Solace

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] sits with me through the night in the library, reading aloud from the books of Verena. Justice, wisdom, patience. By dawn the weight on my heart has lifted, and for the first time in months I can think clearly.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] leads me to a quiet chapel of the Lady and bids me keep a vigil until sunrise. I kneel before the image of the Lady in the silence, and some time in the night the knot inside me comes undone.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] takes my hands in his rough old ones and prays over me, rocking back and forth and murmuring the old words of Ursun and Dazh. It should seem absurd. Instead, I weep like a child, and afterwards I feel lighter than I have in years.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] recites the words of the Prophets beside the Holy Flame while I sit and listen. Line after line, the old verses wash over me until my troubles seem as small as grains of sand in the desert.

[court_sage.GetTitledFirstName] teaches me to sit still, to breathe and to let my thoughts drift past like clouds over the mountains. It takes many days. At the end of them my mind is calm as a pool of water.
I am at peace.
The Serpent's Eye
A diamond the size of a hen's egg, said to have been pried from the eye of a serpent-idol deep in the jungles of Lustria. Its owners never prosper for long.
Crown of the Serpent's Eye
A crown set with the Serpent's Eye, a diamond the size of a hen's egg pried from a serpent-idol in Lustria. Its wearers never prosper for long.

A sea captain back from the western ocean begs an audience and lays a bundle of sailcloth before my throne. Inside is a diamond the size of a hen's egg, blazing with green fire. He swears it was pried from the eye of a great stone serpent in a jungle temple of Lustria, and that the man who took it died screaming the same night. He wants only to be rid of it, for a modest price.

A human trader has come to my hold with a diamond the size of a hen's egg, pried, so he says, from the eye of a stone serpent in Lustria. The moment I see it the hall falls away. It is perfect. No umgi should ever have touched it. My hands are shaking, and some old, cold part of me remembers the tales of the gold-sickness.
Have it set in a crown worthy of it.
Lock it in the treasury.
A gift for my beloved.
I want nothing to do with it. Sell it.
The new crown is finished at last, and the Serpent's Eye blazes from its brow. When I wear it into the hall, every head turns.
Magnificent.
The guards caught a thief in my bedchamber in the dead of night, his hand already on the crown. He died in the struggle before he could say who sent him.
I will not sleep easily again.
As I rode out today the sun caught the Serpent's Eye, and a flash of green fire struck the eyes of the warhorse beside me. It reared, screaming, and threw its rider among the courtiers.
Fetch the physicians!
[From.GetTitledFirstName] came at me in the corridor with a knife, eyes fixed not on my face but on the crown. The guards cut [From.GetHerHim] down before the blade found my heart.
What possessed [From.GetHerHim]?
The Serpent's Eye lies on a velvet cushion in my treasury. Somehow it seems to glow even in the dark.
It is the finest thing I own.

I find myself in the treasury more and more often, just to look at the Serpent's Eye. Sometimes whole days pass. The courtiers whisper that I have grown strange and pale, and that I talk to the diamond when I think no one is listening. Let them whisper. It is mine. My precious.

The gold-sickness has me, as it took the kings of old. I sit for days in the vault with the Serpent's Eye, counting its facets, and when my kin come to fetch me I snarl at them like a cornered beast. My beard has grown tangled and grey. Let them talk. It is mine.
Mine. Mine. All mine.
The treasury has been broken into. The guards are dead, the locks are untouched, and the Serpent's Eye is gone. Nothing else was taken.
Find the thief! Find them!
I lie awake every night listening for footsteps near the treasury. Every servant looks like a thief, every guest like a spy. The Serpent's Eye is safe, I know it is, but I cannot stop worrying.
I must check on it again.
[gem_spouse.GetFirstName] was robbed in the market today. The thieves took nothing but the Serpent's Eye, and vanished into the crowd.
At least [gem_spouse.GetSheHe] is safe.

[gem_spouse.GetFirstName] has not let the Serpent's Eye out of [gem_spouse.GetHerHis] sight for months. Now [gem_spouse.GetSheHe] talks to it, laughs with it, and screams at anyone who comes near. The physicians say there is nothing they can do.
What have I given [gem_spouse.GetHerHim]?

Robbers broke into our chambers in the night and murdered [gem_spouse.GetFirstName] in [gem_spouse.GetHerHis] bed. Yet when the guards searched the room, they found the Serpent's Eye lying untouched under the pillow, glittering.
Merciful gods.

My advisers have begun to whisper what I have long suspected: the Serpent's Eye is cursed. Ever since it came to me there has been nothing but misfortune. The old sailors say the serpent gods of Lustria never forgive a theft.
Sell it to the first buyer who will take it.
Throw it in the river.
Nonsense. I am keeping it.
No one will ever take it from me. No one.
The merchants who bought the Serpent's Eye left a month ago. I think about it every day. Perhaps I acted too hastily.
Send riders after them. Bring it back.
No. Let it go.
My riders caught the merchants on the road and took back the Serpent's Eye by force, without returning a penny. All the realm is calling me a thief. I do not care. It is back where it belongs.
Mine again.
I watched the Serpent's Eye sink into the river a month ago. Now I dream of it every night, glowing green in the mud at the bottom.
Drag the river. I must have it back.
It is better this way.
For days I stood waist-deep in the cold river with the searchers, sifting the mud with my own hands. We found nothing but stones, and I came home soaked to the bone and shivering.
It is gone forever.
This morning the Serpent's Eye was gone. No locks were broken and no guards saw anything. Someone close to me must have taken it, and someone must pay.
My spouse took it. I know it.
It was my sibling. Who else?
One of my councillors is the thief.
Some courtier did this.
Perhaps it is better gone.
[gem_blamed.GetTitledFirstName] stands before me in chains, pale and protesting innocence. There is no proof. There is only my certainty.
Release [gem_blamed.GetHerHim]. I was wrong.
Guilty. Take [gem_blamed.GetHerHim] to the block.
When the treasury was opened after [From.GetTitledFirstName]'s death, the Serpent's Eye was nowhere to be found. No one knows where it went. Perhaps it has gone looking for a new owner.
Good riddance.
The Young Champion

A young man rides through the gates today on a horse too good for his patched cloak, with a notched sword at his hip and nothing else to his name. He kneels before my throne and says that he has heard of me in every tavern from here to the border, that he has no lord and wants none but the best, and that he will follow me to the end of the world if I let him.\n\nMy captains snigger. Then one of them is foolish enough to test him in the yard, and nobody sniggers any more.

A young Dawi came to the hold today, his beard barely past his belt and his armour handed down from his grandfather's grandfather. He stood before my throne with his axe on his shoulder and told me that he had come to make a name worth carving in stone, and that only in my service would he find the battles to do it.\n\nThe old warriors laughed into their beards. Then he beat three of them on the practice floor in a row, and the hall went quiet.

A big young orc came stomping into camp today. He'z still got all his teef and dragged a dead troll behind him on a rope, and he says he heard I'm da biggest, meanest boss for a hundred miles and he wants to fight for me 'cos dat's where da best fightin' iz.\n\nSome of da lads tried to krump him for his cheek. Dey're still pickin' demselves up.

A young elf came to court today, a warrior barely out of his first century, in armour polished to a mirror shine. He bowed deeply and said that the sagas told of great lords and great deeds, that he meant to be part of one, and that he had chosen my service as the likeliest place to find them.\n\nThe courtiers smiled at his arrogance. Then the swordmasters watched him spar, and stopped smiling.
Rise. You will ride at my side.
A young champion of great promise joins your court.
I have warriors enough. Find another lord.

[From.GetFirstName] has been at court for a year now. He is always at my side, at the hunt and the table and in the council, and he has a way of saying aloud what everyone else is too careful to say. I find I look for him when he is not there.
A true friend is rarer than gold.
The Champion's Renown

The camp talks of nothing but [From.GetFirstName]. In the thick of the battle he cut his way through to the enemy banner, threw down its bearer and held the standard aloft until our line rallied around him. The soldiers are already singing songs about it, and every one of them is a little louder than the last.
That is my champion!
A Hero's Death

We won the day, but [fallen_champion.GetFirstName] is dead. He was at the front where he always was, and when the enemy line broke he rode after them alone, too far and too fast. They found him at dusk on a heap of the enemy dead, his sword broken in his hand.\n\nThe soldiers carried him back on their shields. Tonight they do not sing.

The battle is lost, and [fallen_champion.GetFirstName] lost with it. When the line broke he did not run. He turned his horse around, called for anyone who would follow him, and held the ford long enough for the rest of the army to escape. Those who came back say they heard him laughing to the end.\n\nAll that came back of him was his horn, still bloody.
He will be remembered as long as songs are sung.
